I am researching a federal dataset. Dataset title: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP)
Description: The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), managed by the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), helps keep families safe and healthy through initiatives that assist families with energy costs. The LIHEAP compiles national- and state-level program data reported by grant recipients and tracks information on the funding, usage, and effectiveness of federal block grants that help low-income households cover home heating and cooling costs. It provides comprehensive statistics on home energy assistance, household demographics, and the performance measures of grant recipients.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Background and Purpose — More information on the Annual LIHEAP Report to Congress.

Each year, the Office of Community Services publishes the LIHEAP Report to Congress, as required by Section 2610(a)(4) and (5) and section 2610(b) of the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program Act (42 U.S.C. 8629).

The LIHEAP Report to Congress provides information regarding the following:
• Sources and uses of LIHEAP funding
• Amount, cost and type of fuels used by LIHEAP eligible households
• Type of fuel used by various income groups
• Number and income levels of households assisted with LIHEAP
• Household LIHEAP benefit levels
• LIHEAP offset of average heating costs
• Number of LIHEAP assisted households that include vulnerable members
• LIHEAP recipiency targeting performance measures

Data for this report are collected from a variety of sources. For example, fiscal data is obtained from the Office of Community Services, while data regarding LIHEAP assisted households is compiled from grant recipient reports. Other data sources include the American Community Survey and Residential Energy Consumption Survey. More information regarding data collection activities can be found in Appendix A of each Report to Congress.

Information from the Report to Congress is used for Congressional oversight and in response to Congressional and White House queries. Data included in the Report to Congress can also be accessed through the Data Warehouse.

Data Case Studies

LIHEAP Data Case Studies

LIHEAP Glossary
Site Feedback

The Data Case Studies page allows users to access examples of using data for performance management, prepared by the Performance Management Implementation Work Group (PMIWG). The data case studies include reports and tutorials, webinars, tools, and short videos demonstrating ways grant recipients have utilized data to examine their programs.

Have a question? Users can also submit feedback or request additional data case studies.

Applying Automation to Improve Program Processes.

Examining Software Automation in Kansas - Data Case Study #4 - January 14, 2025
This video features representatives from Kansas Department for Children and Families as they discuss Kansas' effort to automate software for improved LIHEAP application processing.

Combining LIHEAP and Census Data.

Using LIHEAP and Census Data for Geographic Analysis - Data Case Study #3 - YouTube - April 7, 2023
This is a short video about Illinois' effort to use LIHEAP Data and Census Data to analyze the share of the income-eligible population served by LIHEAP.

Instructions: Using LIHEAP and Census Data for Geographic Analysis - PDF Document - June 9, 2023

Using Data for Geospatial Analysis.

Using Geospatial Data for Targeting LIHEAP Assistance in Washington - Data Case Study #2 - Youtube - June 17, 2023
This is a short video about Washington's efforts to use LIHEAP geospatial data to review and conduct targeted program outreach .

Targeting Vulnerable Households.

LIHEAP Data Case Study: Targeting Energy Assistance to Vulnerable Populations - Youtube - July 13, 2020
This is a short video about how LIHEAP coordinators can use program data to target outreach efforts to vulnerable households.

LIHEAP Data Case Study: Changes in Targeting Vulnerable Populations Over Time - PDF Document - 2017
This case study examines how Indiana has served its income-eligible population and vulnerable low-income households over time. The appendix provides a tutorial for other states to access the same information about their programs using the Data Warehouse.

Targeting Households with High Energy Burdens.

LIHEAP Data Case Study: Energy Burden Targeting - PDF Document - 2017
This case study examines how Minnesota's benefit determination procedures targets benefits and burden reduction for households with high energy burdens using program outcomes from FY 2016. The appendix provides a tutorial for other states to access the same information about their programs using the Data Warehouse.

Training Webinar: LIHEAP Performance Management — Using Data to Inform Benefit Determination Procedures and Program Coordination - Youtube - September 2, 2020
This webinar presents information on how states can use data to inform their benefit determination procedures and better understand the interaction between LIHEAP and other energy assistance programs.

Training Webinar: Understanding How to Use Performance Data for Program Assessment - Youtube - March 27, 2019
This webinar provides an overview of how state grant recipients can assess their program performance using data.

LIHEAP Performance Management: Data Informed Program Decisions – Youtube - December 2, 2021
This one-hour Webinar will provide a review of the Iowa Case Study, completed by the Performance Management Implementation Work Group (PMIWG), to demonstrate to grant recipients how they can use their own program data to model and assess the potential impact of program changes.

Using Data for Program Planning and Forecasting.

This tool can be used to provide key insights into the topic of program planning and forecasting. The tool allows grant recipients to enter their own, historic data on program applications and approvals to forecast applications for the remainder of the fiscal year. The tool contains a tutorial with instructions to help grant recipients use it.

Welcome to the LIHEAP Performance Management Website

This federal website provides resources, tools, and a dynamic Data Warehouse to help local program administrators, policymakers, and the public access performance management information and performance measurement data for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP).

  • What's New in July 2026


    • New for July
      • APPRISE conducted a webinar on June 16th about the FY26 Quarterly Reports that reviewed the changes made to this year's reports.
        • The slide deck and webinar video will be uploaded to the Required Reports and the LIHEAP Training Webinars pages.
      • Preliminary Fiscal Year 2025 state data have been uploaded to the LIHEAP Data Warehouse.
      • Fiscal Year 2025 Grant Recipient Profiles and Performance Measures Executive Summaries are uploaded on the Performance Measures page and the Data Warehouse.

  • Access Reports to Congress and 1-Page Grant Recipient Profiles

    The Reports to Congress page includes the most recent published annual LIHEAP Reports to Congress and 1-page Grant Recipient Profiles that provide a snapshot of each Grant Recipient's LIHEAP program using 2014 Report to Congress Data.

    The Report to Congress provides detailed national and state-level information on LIHEAP each year. This includes:

    • Fiscal Data
    • Home Energy Data
    • Household Data
    • Program Implementation Data
    • Data Collection Activities
    • Performance Measurement

  • Create Reports and Analyze Data

    The LIHEAP Data Warehouse contains data reported by grant recipients and developed by the Office of Community Services (OCS) since 2001. The Data Warehouse has four different options for accessing data:
    • The Grant Recipient Profiles tool allows you to access 1-page profiles for each LIHEAP state grant recipient, compiled using annual LIHEAP data.
    • The Standard Reports tool provides you with step-by-step guidance in accessing LIHEAP data and creating data reports, tables, and graphs. This tool contains information on national and state level LIHEAP program statistics and allows cross-state comparisons.
    • The Custom Reports tool allows you to develop and download more complex tables and graphics using LIHEAP program data reported by grant recipients and other data on low-income households made available by OCS.
    • The Resources and Tutorial tab contains information about how to use the data warehouse and its data sources.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP)
Description: The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), managed by the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), helps keep families safe and healthy through initiatives that assist families with energy costs. The LIHEAP compiles national- and state-level program data reported by grant recipients and tracks information on the funding, usage, and effectiveness of federal block grants that help low-income households cover home heating and cooling costs. It provides comprehensive statistics on home energy assistance, household demographics, and the performance measures of grant recipients.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Research report: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) data

**Research date:** October 9, 2026  
**Principal federal source:** [LIHEAP Performance Management website and Data Warehouse](https://liheappm.acf.gov/)

## Executive assessment

Your description is **substantially accurate**, but the title needs an important qualification: **LIHEAP is a federal assistance program, not one discrete dataset.** Its public data are a collection of administrative reports, survey-derived estimates, performance measures, downloadable tables, and publications, principally disseminated through the **LIHEAP Data Warehouse**.

The collection is particularly valuable for studying funding, households served, benefit levels, program reach, and targeting of vulnerable or high-energy-burden households. It is **not a public household-level recipient database**, and its performance indicators do not, by themselves, establish causal effects on health, poverty, or long-term energy security.

Three distinctions are essential:

1. **Program coverage is broader than warehouse coverage.** LIHEAP funds states, the District of Columbia, participating tribes and tribal organizations, and territories. Warehouse documentation principally describes **state and DC data**, excluding separately reported tribal data.
2. **Reporting obligations differ by recipient type.** States and DC submit the Performance Data Form; tribes and territories do not complete that form. Household reporting has separate long and short forms.
3. **Publication dates differ across products.** At this review, the website announced preliminary **FY2025 warehouse data**, while its Reports to Congress page identified **FY2022** as the most recent report.

For cataloging, I recommend the descriptive title:

> **LIHEAP Data Warehouse and associated federal program reporting data**

This is a recommended catalog title, not a verified official catalog-record title.

---

## 1. Dataset identity and scope

| Attribute | Findings |
|---|---|
| Program name | Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program—LIHEAP |
| Main public data service | LIHEAP Data Warehouse, on the LIHEAP Performance Management website |
| Federal steward | U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), Administration for Children and Families (ACF), Office of Community Services (OCS) |
| Responsible program office | Division of Energy Assistance |
| Data character | Aggregated administrative program data, federal fiscal records, survey-derived eligible-population estimates, and calculated performance indicators |
| Principal geography | States and District of Columbia; national aggregates; some related publications include regional analysis |
| Main temporal coverage | Warehouse data beginning in FY2001; coverage varies by variable |
| Main reporting frequency | Annual, with related quarterly reporting |
| Statistical unit | Primarily households, funding amounts, and state/program-level aggregates—not individual people |
| Access | Public warehouse access does not require registration; some recipient-specific preliminary access is restricted |
| Documented export | CSV/Excel-readable table export; downloadable charts and PDF publications |
| Latest warehouse announcement observed | Preliminary FY2025 state data |
| Latest congressional report identified on reviewed page | FY2022 |
| Important exclusions | No verified public nationwide recipient microdata; warehouse is not a complete representation of separately administered tribal and territorial programs |

Sources: [warehouse overview](https://liheappm.acf.gov/), [tutorial](https://liheappm.acf.gov/data_warehouse/doc/tutorial.pdf), [help](https://liheappm.acf.gov/help), and [Reports to Congress](https://liheappm.acf.gov/reports_to_congress).

### A more precise description

> The LIHEAP public data collection, administered by HHS/ACF’s Office of Community Services, combines annual grant-recipient reports, federal funding information, and survey-derived estimates to describe home-energy assistance funding, households served, benefit levels, eligible-population coverage, and performance. The principal public warehouse provides state/DC and aggregated national statistics beginning in FY2001, with variable-specific historical coverage. It includes indicators of energy-burden reduction, benefit targeting, and restoration or prevention of loss of home-energy service. Public warehouse data are aggregated rather than recipient-level records.

This retains the substance of your description while avoiding an implication that the collection is a complete causal evaluation or a census of all LIHEAP jurisdictions.

---

## 2. Who publishes, produces, and maintains it?

### Federal responsibility

The federal chain of responsibility is:

**HHS → ACF → OCS → Division of Energy Assistance.**

OCS administers the federal program, collects or oversees recipient reporting, develops associated statistics, and publishes the congressional reports and public data products.

### Original data producers

The collection draws on several distinct producers:

- **State and other grant-recipient agencies:** administrative records of assistance, household characteristics, benefits, and program operations.
- **OCS:** allocations and other fiscal information.
- **U.S. Census Bureau:** estimates of low-income and income-eligible households.
- **Energy Information Administration (EIA):** Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) information used in related energy-cost and consumption analyses.

The [Reports to Congress page](https://liheappm.acf.gov/reports_to_congress) explicitly identifies OCS fiscal data, recipient reports, the American Community Survey (ACS), and RECS as sources.

### Contractor and technical roles

The website footer attributes development to **APPRISE Incorporated, NCAT, Verve Associates, Z Federal, and iData Technologies**, and identifies HHS contract **HHSP233201500094I** as funding the website.

APPRISE also:

- Reviews submitted Performance Data Forms;
- Helps recipients resolve reporting issues;
- Provides training and technical assistance;
- Manages the performance-management help desk.

These organizations should be recorded as technical contributors where appropriate, **not substituted for HHS/ACF/OCS as the federal publisher**. The footer is evidence of the stated development arrangement, not proof that every named organization remains an active contractor today.

Sources: [warehouse website](https://liheappm.acf.gov/datawarehouse), [FY2024 Performance Data Form instructions transmittal](https://acf.gov/ocs/policy-guidance/liheap-2025-02-liheap-performance-data-form-fiscal-year-fy-2024), [help desk](https://liheappm.acf.gov/help-desk).

---

## 3. Legal authority and reporting mandate

This collection has a direct statutory foundation—not merely a general open-data rationale.

### Program authority

LIHEAP was established by **Title XXVI of the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1981, Public Law 97-35**, as amended, and is codified in **42 U.S.C. Chapter 94**, beginning at §8621.

### Data collection: 42 U.S.C. §8629(a)

Section 2610(a) of the LIHEAP Act requires the HHS Secretary, after consultation with the Secretary of Energy, to provide for collection of information concerning:

- Home-energy consumption;
- Amount, cost, and types of fuel used by eligible households;
- Fuel types used by different income groups;
- Numbers and income levels of assisted households;
- Assisted households containing older people, disabled members, or young children;
- Other information reasonably necessary to administer the program.

The provision permits use of information already collected by other federal agencies.

### Annual report to Congress: §8629(b)

The statute requires an annual report to Congress, **no later than June 30**, compiling prior-fiscal-year data and describing program implementation and impact.

**Important:** this is the statutory deadline. It should not be mistaken for a guarantee that the public report or warehouse release appears by that date.

### Recipient reporting and performance measurement

Other relevant provisions include:

- **42 U.S.C. §8624(b)(14):** recipients must cooperate with federal data collection and reporting.
- **§8624(c)(1)(G):** household application and receipt information is part of the grant-application reporting framework.
- **§8624(b)(5):** assistance should prioritize households with the lowest incomes and highest energy costs or needs relative to income.
- **1994 amendments:** directed HHS to develop model performance goals and measurements in consultation with grant recipients.

Household reporting instructions also cite **45 CFR §96.82**.

Primary legal sources: [ACF statute and regulations](https://acf.gov/ocs/policy-guidance/laws-regulations/liheap) and [U.S. Code, Chapter 94](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?edition=prelim&path=%2Fprelim%40title42%2Fchapter94).

### Paperwork Reduction Act identifiers

These identify information collections, **not dataset accession numbers**:

| Collection | OMB control number |
|---|---|
| LIHEAP Household Report | **0970-0060** |
| LIHEAP Performance Data Form | **0970-0449** |
| Carryover and Reallotment Report | **0970-0106** |
| Quarterly Performance and Management Report | **0970-0589** |

The FY2026 Household Report instructions show approval through **March 31, 2029**. Other reviewed documents contain older approval dates, including an expired date for the Performance Data Form. Consequently, librarians should preserve each form’s approval information by version and verify current approval independently rather than copy an old date into a current catalog record.

Sources: [FY2026 Household Report long-form instructions](https://acf.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ocs/ATT.3.COMM_LIHEAP_AT2025_HHR_LongFormInstr_FY26.pdf), [FY2026 supplemental grant terms](https://acf.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ocse/OCS-93.568-LIHEAP-TC-FY26-Final-4.22.2026.pdf).

---

## 4. History and major changes

| Period | Significance |
|---|---|
| **1981** | LIHEAP established; statutory energy-assistance data collection and reporting framework began. |
| **1984 onward** | Amendments changed the collection and congressional-reporting provisions. |
| **1994** | Congress clarified emphasis on households with the lowest incomes and high energy burdens; expanded household reporting and model performance measurement requirements. |
| **FY2001** | Beginning of the historical series described for the current warehouse. This is **not** the program’s founding date or a verified warehouse launch date. |
| **FY2006** | State eligible-population estimation shifted from CPS-based estimates to ACS-based estimates. |
| **FY2011** | Historical warehouse inventory identifies the beginning of “any assistance” unduplicated total-household counts and certain combined vulnerability fields. |
| **FY2015–2016** | Eligible-population estimation used averages of annual ACS PUMS files after Census discontinued three-year ACS products. |
| **FY2016** | States/DC began required reporting of expanded performance measures concerning energy burden, targeting, and energy-service continuity. |
| **FY2017 onward** | State eligible-population estimates use five-year ACS PUMS. |
| **Pandemic and supplemental-funding years** | CARES Act, ARPA, and other supplemental funding introduced additional reporting categories and complications for trend analysis. |
| **FY2026 reporting** | Household instructions remove CARES/ARPA reporting sections and make other form changes. |
| **Current reviewed website** | Announces preliminary FY2025 data and FY2025 profiles; congressional-report page identifies FY2022 as its latest report. |

The FY2014 Report to Congress describes itself as the **32nd annual report** on HHS energy-assistance programs. Older publications therefore extend the documentary record well before the warehouse’s FY2001 starting point.

Sources: [FY2014 congressional report](https://acf.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ocs/fy14_liheap_rtc_final.pdf), [FY2016 performance report](https://liheappm.acf.gov/sites/default/files/private/notebooks/2016/HEN_Part3_Perf%20Meas_FY2016.pdf), [eligibility methodology](https://liheappm.acf.gov/eligibility-methodology), and [historical field inventory](https://liheappm.acf.gov/DW-tutorial-supplements).

**Unresolved:** I did not establish an exact original warehouse launch date or a complete history of its software migrations.

---

## 5. What the collection contains

### A. Household Report data

These describe households assisted, generally by:

- Heating assistance;
- Cooling assistance;
- Crisis assistance;
- LIHEAP-funded weatherization;
- Other reportable assistance categories, depending on year.

Household characteristics include:

- Income or poverty intervals;
- Members age 60 or older;
- Members with disabilities;
- Children age five or younger;
- Presence of any vulnerable member.

Newer reporting forms also include additional characteristics, such as owner/renter status. **A field’s presence on a reporting form does not establish that it is available in the warehouse for every year.**

The FY2026 long form applies to the 50 states, DC, and Puerto Rico. Direct-grant tribes, tribal organizations, and other territories use the short form.

### B. Performance Data Form—Module 1

The grant-recipient survey covers:

- Sources of funds;
- Uses of funds;
- Average benefit levels;
- Income eligibility limits;
- Program-component information.

### C. Required performance modules

For states/DC, these cover:

- Energy-burden targeting;
- Restoration of home-energy service;
- Prevention of loss of home-energy service.

An additional module permits optional reporting.

### D. Eligible-population estimates

These estimate income-eligible households under:

1. Federal maximum income guidelines;
2. State-specific income guidelines.

They support calculations of program reach and targeting.

### E. Related publications

The broader collection includes:

- Annual Reports to Congress and supplemental tables;
- Home Energy Notebooks and separately published sections;
- State profiles;
- Performance-measure summaries;
- Special studies;
- Reporting instructions, glossaries, training, and data case studies.

Sources: [required reports](https://liheappm.acf.gov/required-reports/), [FY2024 Performance Data Form transmittal](https://acf.gov/ocs/policy-guidance/liheap-2025-02-liheap-performance-data-form-fiscal-year-fy-2024), [inventory documents](https://liheappm.acf.gov/DW-tutorial-supplements).

---

## 6. How the data are produced and validated

The basic reporting process is:

**Local administrative records → recipient aggregation → OLDC submission → federal/contractor review → correction or revision → public release.**

Recipients submit reports through ACF’s **Online Data Collection system (OLDC)**, a component of GrantSolutions.

Documented checks include consistency among:

- Household Reports;
- Performance Data Forms;
- State Model Plans;
- Quarterly reports;
- Carryover and Reallotment Reports;
- Federal Financial Reports, where relevant.

For example, reported cooling obligations should be consistent with reported cooling assistance and the approved program plan. Recipients are instructed to explain missing data and inconsistencies in notes and can submit revisions.

Sources: [required reports](https://liheappm.acf.gov/required-reports/) and [FY2026 household instructions](https://acf.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ocs/ATT.3.COMM_LIHEAP_AT2025_HHR_LongFormInstr_FY26.pdf).

### Administrative and survey data must be distinguished

Recipient counts are administrative aggregates. Eligible-population denominators are **survey-derived estimates**.

The methodology page documents:

- CPS ASEC averages for FY2001–2005;
- ACS sources beginning in FY2006;
- Different pooling periods across subsequent years;
- Five-year ACS PUMS beginning with FY2017;
- FY2025 estimates based on **2020–2024 ACS**.

It also notes a disability-definition issue affecting FY2009 estimates.

This means an apparent change in coverage can reflect **a denominator-method change**, not just program performance. The reviewed year-by-year methodology list also omits FY2022; that omission should be clarified with the publisher rather than filled by assumption.

Source: [eligible-population methodology](https://liheappm.acf.gov/eligibility-methodology).

---

## 7. Definitions and performance measures

### Household

LIHEAP counts a **household**, not a beneficiary person. The statutory definition centers on individuals living together as an economic unit for whom residential energy is purchased in common, including energy paid through rent.

### Energy burden

Conceptually:

\[
\text{Energy burden}=\frac{\text{annual residential energy costs}}{\text{annual household income}}\times100
\]

Performance forms distinguish burden before and after assistance, percentage-point changes, and percentage reductions. These are not interchangeable.

For aggregate reproduction, use the applicable year’s calculation guide: a ratio of aggregate averages need not equal the average of individual household ratios.

### Targeting indices

- **Recipiency targeting index:** compares a group’s share of recipients with its share of income-eligible households.
- **Benefit targeting index:** compares average benefits for high-burden households with average benefits for all measured recipient households.
- **Burden-reduction targeting index:** compares the measured proportional burden reduction for high-burden households with that for the overall measured group.

An index of **100** represents parity with the reference group. Above or below 100 indicates greater or lesser targeting under that particular measure—not a percentage of all eligible households served.

Historical guidance defines high-burden households using the **highest-burden quartile** of the relevant measured households. Definitions, inclusion rules, zero-income handling, and calculation methods should be checked by year.

Sources: [field-by-field performance guide](https://www.liheappm.acf.gov/sites/default/files/private/pm/LIHEAP-PM-Field-by-Field-Definitions-V1.0.pdf) and [FY2017 performance reporting training](https://liheappm.acf.gov/sites/default/files/private/training/pm_webinar/Step-By-Step-Overview-FY-2017-PDF-Module-2-PM.pdf).

---

## 8. Major analytical limitations

These are the most consequential cautions for research and advocacy.

### Do not add assistance categories to estimate unique households

A household may receive heating and crisis assistance in the same year. Counts can be unduplicated **within each category** but overlap **across categories**.

Use the reported “any assistance” unduplicated count when available. The historical inventory places that series at FY2011 onward.

### Vulnerability categories overlap

One household can contain an older adult, a disabled member, and a young child. Adding those categories will overcount vulnerable households.

### Obligations are not expenditures

The Performance Data Form guidance expressly states that “uses of funds” represents **obligations**, not necessarily money spent during the same fiscal year. Some general website documentation uses looser language. For fiscal analysis, the year-specific reporting instructions should control.

### Federal fiscal years differ from state program years

Federal FY2026 runs **October 1, 2025–September 30, 2026**. States may operate a different program year but must report for the federal period.

### State rankings require context

States differ in:

- Climate and fuel mix;
- Energy prices;
- Eligibility policies;
- Assistance components;
- Benefit formulas;
- Housing conditions;
- Reporting systems and completeness.

A larger benefit or higher index does not automatically mean a better-run program.

### “Income eligible” does not mean fully program eligible

Survey estimates cannot necessarily account for every administrative eligibility condition. “Percent served” is therefore not a precise count of all legally eligible applicants who were denied assistance.

### Performance data may cover a subset

Measures requiring complete income, benefit, and energy-bill information may not represent every assisted household. National results may use only states with usable data. Preserve coverage notes and sample counts.

### Missing is not zero

Distinguish:

- Not applicable;
- Not collected;
- Not reported;
- Incomplete;
- Not yet public;
- True zero.

### Public national aggregates may not cover every jurisdiction

An “all states” total is not necessarily a total of state, tribal, and territorial LIHEAP programs combined.

### These are not causal impact estimates

Arithmetic burden reduction and reported restoration/prevention counts are useful operational indicators. Alone, they do not establish reductions in mortality, hospitalizations, evictions, or future disconnections.

Sources: [household instructions](https://acf.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ocs/ATT.3.COMM_LIHEAP_AT2025_HHR_LongFormInstr_FY26.pdf), [Performance Data Form guidance](https://acf.gov/ocs/policy-guidance/liheap-2025-02-liheap-performance-data-form-fiscal-year-fy-2024), [warehouse help](https://liheappm.acf.gov/data-warehouse-help).

---

## 9. Typical users and public benefits

### Documented users

The publisher identifies:

- LIHEAP administrators and grant recipients;
- Policymakers;
- Congress and White House staff;
- The public.

Other well-supported uses include academic research, journalism, public-interest advocacy, and utility-affordability analysis.

### Documented applications

The [data case studies](https://liheappm.acf.gov/data_case_studies) provide concrete examples:

| Example | Application |
|---|---|
| Indiana | Tracking assistance to vulnerable households over time |
| Minnesota | Examining benefit determination and targeting of high-burden households |
| Illinois | Combining LIHEAP and Census data to examine geographic coverage |
| Washington | Geospatial analysis for targeted outreach |
| Iowa | Modeling potential program changes using recipient data |
| Application Projection Tool | Forecasting applications and approvals |

Some of these require a state’s own detailed administrative data, **not just public warehouse tables**.

### Benefits to the public

The data enable:

- **Accountability:** understanding how public funding is allocated and obligated.
- **Program improvement:** adjusting outreach, benefit formulas, and program components.
- **Equity assessment:** identifying under-service of vulnerable populations.
- **Informed advocacy:** examining funding adequacy and assistance reach.
- **Historical research:** documenting changes across decades.
- **Public understanding:** making complex block-grant administration more legible.

These are benefits of the **data infrastructure**. They should be distinguished from the program’s direct benefits—help with energy bills, crisis intervention, and related services.

---

## 10. Access, formats, documentation, and rights

### Access routes

Start with:

1. [Data Warehouse](https://liheappm.acf.gov/datawarehouse);
2. Standard Reports for guided comparisons;
3. [Custom Reports](https://liheappm.acf.gov/datawarehouse/custom_reports);
4. [Reports to Congress](https://liheappm.acf.gov/reports_to_congress);
5. [Performance Measures](https://liheappm.acf.gov/performance-measures);
6. [Field inventories](https://liheappm.acf.gov/DW-tutorial-supplements).

Older documentation uses names such as “Guided Search” and “Advanced Data & Analytics.” These are useful historical aliases, not proof of separate datasets.

### Formats and technical access

Documentation explicitly supports **CSV/Excel-readable table exports** and chart downloads. Related materials include PDFs, spreadsheets, Word templates, videos, and macro-enabled planning tools.

I did **not** verify:

- A documented public API;
- A complete bulk database download;
- A permanent federal dataset identifier;
- A dataset-wide DOI;
- Total row counts or file size;
- A formal public release/versioning policy.

The warehouse page is JavaScript-driven. Retrieving its HTML alone returned an application shell rather than the statistical tables. This matters for harvesting and preservation.

### Documentation quality

The field inventories map names to definitions, report sections, historical availability, and required/calculated status. They are valuable but include documents dated **2017 and 2020**. Current year-specific forms should supplement them.

### Rights and licensing

Public access and documented export are established. I did not locate a clear collection-wide license in the reviewed federal warehouse documentation.

Federal government works are generally outside U.S. copyright protection under 17 U.S.C. §105, but contractor-produced material and third-party content may require separate review. Do not automatically label the whole website CC0 or Creative Commons.

A similarly named California dataset on Data.gov carries a CC-BY license. **That state dataset’s license must not be transferred to the federal collection.**

### Privacy

Public warehouse statistics are aggregate data. A separate **2024–2025 RECS–LIHEAP administrative data-match project**, announced in June 2026, requests household-level records for matching. That project should be cataloged separately and does not imply public availability of identifiable recipient records.

Source: [2026 RECS data-match announcement](https://acf.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ocs/COMM_LIHEAP_RECSDataMatchAT_FY2025_06252026.pdf).

---

## 11. Preservation priorities and recommended archival package

**Preservation assessment:** high public value, with meaningful technical and interpretive fragility.

The reviewed site was available; I found no evidence that the entire collection has disappeared. The concern is that a live, revisable, JavaScript-based service is not itself a durable archival object.

### Priority risks

- Dynamic tables may escape ordinary web crawls.
- Preliminary values can be revised.
- PDFs and warehouse tables can represent different releases.
- Form fields and funding categories change.
- Older documentation can remain online beside newer instructions.
- Agency domains and file paths can change.
- Footnotes may be lost during conversion.
- Macro-enabled tools can become unusable as software changes.

### Recommended preservation package

Preserve together:

1. **Original exports**, by year and data source.
2. **Congressional reports and all supplemental tables**, including methodological appendices.
3. **Profiles and performance summaries**.
4. **Forms, instructions, OMB information, glossaries, and inventories** for each reporting year.
5. **Provenance manifest:** URL, retrieval date, selections, geographic scope, status, and notes.
6. **Checksums**, preferably SHA-256.
7. **Normalized derivatives**, such as UTF-8 CSV and a documented analytical table.
8. **Transformation code and validation results**.
9. **Browser-rendered captures** of representative reports.
10. **Successive release snapshots**, without overwriting preliminary versions.

For analytical derivatives, record at least:

`fiscal_year`, `jurisdiction`, `jurisdiction_type`, `source_form`, `assistance_type`, `measure`, `value`, `unit`, `population_definition`, `funding_source`, `release_status`, `retrieval_date`, `source_url`, and `notes`.

This is a **recommended preservation schema**, not a verified native warehouse schema.

### Existing third-party preservation lead

Search results identified a DataLumos deposit, **“Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) Data,”** with stated coverage **2001–2025**, version DOI **10.3886/E249275V2**.

The deposit page returned a 403 during direct retrieval, so I could not inspect its files or confirm completeness. Treat it as a useful preservation lead, not a verified replacement for the federal source.

[DataLumos deposit](https://www.datalumos.org/datalumos/project/249275/version/V2/view).

---

## 12. Recommended research and advocacy workflow

1. **Specify the product.** “LIHEAP data” is too broad for reproducibility.
2. **Choose a consistent scope:** state/DC warehouse data versus broader program totals.
3. **Use year-specific definitions and instructions.**
4. **Record preliminary/final status and retrieval date.**
5. **Separate regular and supplemental funding.**
6. **Use unique-household totals instead of adding components.**
7. **Track denominator sources and methodology breaks.**
8. **Adjust dollar trends for inflation**, while retaining nominal values.
9. **Weight national averages appropriately**, rather than averaging state percentages indiscriminately.
10. **Read every relevant footnote.**
11. **Validate exports against published tables** where comparable.
12. **Frame conclusions as descriptive unless the research design supports causality.**

Useful complementary sources include ACS/CPS, RECS, state Model Plans, energy prices, weather data, and state utility-disconnection records. Geographic studies require matching statistical units carefully: **people are not households, ZIP codes are not ZIP Code Tabulation Areas, and survey periods are not necessarily federal fiscal years**.

---

## 13. Contacts, unresolved questions, and research boundaries

### Assistance

- **Data and performance-management help:** [LIHEAP Help Desk](https://liheappm.acf.gov/help-desk), **liheap-support@appriseinc.org**.
- **Website accessibility issues:** **webmaster@ncat.org**, as listed in the site footer.
- **Program and reporting questions:** OCS/Division of Energy Assistance and the relevant regional liaison.

The help desk’s personalized services are primarily described for grant recipients; public researchers should confirm support availability.

### Questions worth asking the publisher

- Is there an official bulk export or supported API?
- Is there a release-by-release revision log?
- What are the retention and archival arrangements?
- What exactly is included in each national aggregate?
- Which variables remain unavailable for some states or years?
- Are sampling uncertainties provided for derived eligible-population measures?
- What is the current Performance Data Form approval status?
- Can a current comprehensive machine-readable dictionary be supplied?
- What rights statement applies to redistributed exports?

### Research boundaries

This report establishes the collection’s institutional, legal, historical, methodological, and preservation context. It is **not a row-level audit**: I did not download and validate every warehouse series, inspect all PDFs in full, or verify the third-party archive’s files. Some PDF findings relied on searchable official-document excerpts because the retrieval tool could not process the PDF directly.

## Bottom line

LIHEAP’s public data are a valuable, legally grounded record of federal energy assistance and state program performance. Their strongest uses are **funding accountability, service-reach analysis, targeting assessment, and program planning**.

For a librarian or preservationist, the central task is to preserve **the reports, definitions, footnotes, and release history alongside the numbers**. For a data scientist or activist, the central discipline is to keep **household counts, survey estimates, obligations, assistance categories, and performance indicators distinct**. Those distinctions determine whether an analysis is reproducible—and whether its conclusions are defensible.

# LIHEAP dataset risk assessment

**Assessment date: October 9, 2026**  
**Scope:** The federal **LIHEAP Data Warehouse and associated reporting products**, principally at [liheappm.acf.gov](https://liheappm.acf.gov/), rather than individual state datasets.

## Overall finding

**LIHEAP data remain publicly available, and collection has not stopped. However, the infrastructure supporting reliable future publication faces substantial staffing and policy risk.** The strongest adverse evidence is the elimination of the dedicated federal LIHEAP staff in April 2025, followed by reassignment of administration to other HHS employees, continued operational concerns, and repeated presidential proposals to eliminate program funding.

There are important counterweights: explicit statutory reporting requirements, continued congressional appropriations, renewed information collections, contractor-supported reporting assistance, and publication of preliminary FY2025 data in July 2026.

**I found no substantiated evidence of deliberate alteration or wholesale removal of historical LIHEAP statistics.** The more evident threat is delayed reporting, incomplete validation, and loss of institutional capacity—not demonstrated falsification.

These ratings distinguish observed conditions from proposed changes. They are not numerical estimates of the probability of deletion.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

- **No Known Issue — supported.** The federal website continues to describe warehouse coverage beginning in **2001**. Its Reports to Congress page retains historical reporting access and profile selections for **2014–2025**. Historical performance reports also remain discoverable at federal URLs, including the [FY2015 performance report](https://liheappm.acf.gov/sites/default/files/private/notebooks/2015/fy2015_hen_perfmeasures.pdf).
- **Moderate Risk — not established for historical records.** Reporting-form revisions remove or replace some fields in future collections, but this is not evidence that previously published historical elements have been deleted.
- **High Risk / Gone — not established.** I found no documented removal of historical files or disappearance of all pre-current-cycle data.

**Sources:** [Warehouse overview](https://liheappm.acf.gov/); [Reports to Congress](https://liheappm.acf.gov/reports_to_congress); [Federal Register reporting-form revisions, April 29, 2025](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/04/29/2025-07375/submission-for-office-of-management-and-budget-omb-review-low-income-home-energy-assistance-program).

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

Historical access remains represented on the primary site, with no identified removal incident.

**Qualification:** This is not a file-by-file or checksum audit. I did not verify every historical export or establish that all values are unchanged. The JavaScript-dependent warehouse also makes comprehensive automated preservation harder than preserving static files.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

- **Moderate Risk — directly supported by reporting delays.** ACF’s FY2026 quarterly-report instructions explicitly state that **OMB approval timing and delayed availability in OLDC required extending Quarter 1 and Quarter 2 deadlines to April 30, 2026**. This is documented collection delay, not merely a forecast.
- **High Risk — a significant concern, but the statutory-deadline trigger is not conclusively verified.** The federal Reports to Congress page still identifies **FY2022** as the latest published report, although the statute requires a report to Congress by June 30 covering the preceding fiscal year. This establishes a public-release backlog. It does **not**, by itself, establish whether later reports were transmitted to Congress but not posted online.
- **No Known Issue — substantial counterevidence.**
  - Preliminary **FY2025 state data** were announced as uploaded in **July 2026**.
  - The Performance Data Form was reinstated and approved on **June 6, 2025**; ACF identifies its expiration as **June 30, 2028**.
  - Reginfo records a further Household Report reinstatement approval on **August 10, 2026**.
  - ACF continues issuing reporting instructions and deadlines.
- **Gone — contradicted.** Collection and publication continue.

**Sources:** [FY2026 quarterly-report action transmittal](https://acf.gov/ocs/policy-guidance/liheap-federal-fiscal-year-2026-fy26-quarterly-report-submission); [July 2026 publication announcement](https://liheappm.acf.gov/); [FY2025 Performance Data Form instructions](https://acf.gov/ocs/policy-guidance/liheap-performance-data-form-federal-fiscal-year-2025-fy25); [Performance Data Form OMB history](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAOMBHistory?ombControlNumber=0970-0449); [Household Report OMB history](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAOMBHistory?ombControlNumber=0970-0060); [Reports to Congress](https://liheappm.acf.gov/reports_to_congress).

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

Actual collection delays meet this threshold. I would raise the rating to **High Risk** if congressional transmission records confirm a missed statutory deadline, or if an annual collection/publication cycle is confirmed skipped.

**Correction to the earlier report:** Old form expiration dates should not be treated as current. Additional research confirms subsequent approvals; there is no basis here for claiming a current ICR expiration exceeding one year.

---

## 3. Data Quality

### Evidence by risk level

- **High Risk — supported on timeliness.** Public finalized congressional reporting substantially trails the more recent preliminary warehouse releases. The documented FY2026 quarterly collection delay also reduces timely availability of administrative information.
- **Moderate Risk — supported on validation capacity and comparability.**
  - Dedicated federal staff losses threaten review, cross-report reconciliation, and institutional knowledge.
  - FY2025 warehouse data remain labeled **preliminary**.
  - Performance Data Form revisions replace CARES/ARPA fiscal categories with IIJA categories and remove maximum-income-cutoff fields from funding uses. These require careful cross-year interpretation.
- **No Known Issue — counterevidence on core content.** The 2025 Federal Register notice preserves annual reporting of funding, average benefits, energy-burden targeting, restoration, and prevention of energy-service loss. FY2026 quarterly revisions also consolidate carryover reporting and make an obligations section mandatory for all recipients, potentially improving coverage.
- **Gone — contradicted.** Reporting remains operational.

**Sources:** [Federal Register, April 29, 2025](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/04/29/2025-07375/submission-for-office-of-management-and-budget-omb-review-low-income-home-energy-assistance-program); [FY2026 quarterly-report instructions](https://acf.gov/ocs/policy-guidance/liheap-federal-fiscal-year-2026-fy26-quarterly-report-submission); [FY2026 reporting-training slides](https://www.liheappm.acf.gov/sites/default/files/private/webinars/2026/FY2026%20Quarterly%20Reports%20Training%20Webinar%20-%207.8.26%20-%20508%20Compliant.pdf); [publication status](https://liheappm.acf.gov/).

### Selected level: **High Risk**

Your rubric includes **reductions in timeliness**, and documented delays and the finalized-report backlog support that designation.

This rating **does not mean the published numbers are proven inaccurate or manipulated**. Evidence of broad reductions in core warehouse granularity or annual frequency is weaker than evidence concerning timeliness.

**Scope caution:** The 2026 RECS–LIHEAP matching request eliminates eight fields, but it is a separate household-level matching collection. Its revisions should not be misrepresented as deletion of eight public warehouse variables. [Federal Register, May 5, 2026](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/05/2026-08689/submission-for-office-of-management-and-budget-review-2024-2025-low-income-home-energy-assistance).

## 4. Statutory Context

### Evidence by risk level

- **No Known Issue — strongly supported.**
  - **42 U.S.C. §8629(a)** explicitly requires collection of energy-consumption, fuel-cost, income, assistance, and vulnerable-household information.
  - **§8629(b)** requires an annual congressional report by June 30.
  - Recipient cooperation and reporting requirements also appear in **§8624**.
  - The data have clear programmatic uses: administration, oversight, targeting, and comparisons among recipients.
- **Moderate Risk — not the best fit.** This is not merely an implied collection needed to administer a program; explicit statutory requirements exist.
- **High Risk — not supported.** ACS and RECS supply complementary information but cannot replace administrative counts, benefit information, and LIHEAP performance reporting.
- **Gone — not applicable under your rubric.**

**Sources:** [U.S. Code, LIHEAP chapter](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?edition=prelim&path=%2Fprelim%40title42%2Fchapter94); [Federal Register explanation of statutory and programmatic uses](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/04/29/2025-07375/submission-for-office-of-management-and-budget-omb-review-low-income-home-energy-assistance-program).

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

The collection has unusually clear legal grounding.

**Important limitation:** The statute protects collection and congressional reporting more directly than it protects the **particular warehouse, its URL, export functions, or indefinite online retention**. Statutory authorization does not guarantee continued operation of this exact public interface.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

### Evidence by risk level

- **High Risk — strongly supported.** Multiple sources reported elimination of the entire dedicated federal LIHEAP team in April 2025. Although sources differ on the count and organizational scope, the reported loss clearly exceeds your **40%** threshold for the dedicated program office.
- **Gone — describes the original team’s reported elimination, but not the current operational system.** Subsequent reporting indicates management was transferred to other HHS employees. The warehouse, contractor assistance, reporting, and grant releases continue.
- **No Known Issue — supported on enacted program funding, not staffing.** Congress provided **$4.045 billion in regular FY2026 funding**, reportedly a $20 million increase over the previous year. Federal tables document actual FY2026 awards and August reallotments.
- **Moderate Risk — understates the dedicated-office staffing disruption.** Proposed elimination budgets are additional threats, but should not be counted as enacted 100% cuts.

**Sources:**
- [NBC News: entire utility-assistance staff eliminated, April 2025](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/business-news/trump-admin-fires-staff-liheap-agency-utilities-assistance-program-rcna199177).
- [NEFI: management transferred to other HHS employees, November 2025](https://nefi.com/news-publications/recent-news/federal-liheap-staff-back-to-work).
- [NEADA: FY2026 funding and continuing staffing concerns](https://neada.org/press/liheap-under-threat/).
- [Federal FY2026 allocation/reallotment table](https://acf.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ocs/LIHEAP-FY26-States-Reallotment-Table.pdf).
- [September 25, 2026 bipartisan congressional request for staffing details](https://pappas.house.gov/media/press-releases/pappas-leads-bipartisan-house-effort-pushing-hhs-to-distribute-liheap-funds).

### Selected level: **High Risk**

The dedicated-team loss meets the high-risk threshold. **Gone** would overstate the present condition because replacement administration and publication demonstrably continue.

The September 2026 congressional letter shows that staffing adequacy remains an unresolved concern; it is not an audited current headcount. Likewise, grant appropriations do not establish how much funding is dedicated to data maintenance.

### Staffing tracker limitation

I reviewed the requested [USAJobs tracker](https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com). It tracks **job advertisements, not staff losses or actual hires**, and announces that collection stopped on **December 31, 2025**. It cannot establish current LIHEAP staffing or reliably quantify the percentage lost. I therefore base this rating on program-specific reporting rather than advertisement counts.

## 6. Policy

### Evidence by risk level

- **High Risk — supported by implemented administrative change.** Elimination of the dedicated program team was a significant actual change, not just a proposal, affecting the capacity supporting data collection, validation, and publication.
- **Moderate Risk — strongly supported by pending funding policy.** The President’s **FY2027 budget again proposes eliminating LIHEAP**, describing a roughly $4 billion reduction and arguing that lower energy prices and state disconnection protections make it unnecessary. These are administration policy claims, not findings adopted in this assessment.
- **No Known Issue — not supported overall.** Continued reporting approvals and appropriations are protective, but do not erase the implemented staffing changes or elimination proposals.
- **Gone — contradicted.** Neither the program’s data collection nor public warehouse publication has been terminated.

**Sources:** [FY2027 President’s Budget, LIHEAP elimination proposal](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/budget_fy2027.pdf); [April 2025 staffing reporting](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/business-news/trump-admin-fires-staff-liheap-agency-utilities-assistance-program-rcna199177); [September 2026 bipartisan congressional intervention](https://pappas.house.gov/media/press-releases/pappas-leads-bipartisan-house-effort-pushing-hhs-to-distribute-liheap-funds).

### Selected level: **High Risk**

Implemented staffing dismantlement meets the rubric’s “other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities” criterion. The proposed funding elimination alone would support **Moderate Risk**, not High Risk.

I found **no verified instruction to erase historical warehouse records, no anti-LIHEAP disclaimer on the warehouse, and no demonstrated presidential-action-driven rewrite of its core statistics**. Routine form changes first proposed in December 2024 should not automatically be attributed to the administration that took office in January 2025.

## Preservation implications

**Priority: preserve now, while access continues.** The immediate practical risk is losing a usable, well-documented and validated series through operational deterioration—even without deliberate deletion.

Preservation should include:

1. Historical and current exports, with preliminary/final status and retrieval dates.
2. Congressional reports, supplemental tables, and detailed footnotes.
3. Each year’s reporting forms, definitions, methodologies, and OMB approvals.
4. Successive snapshots and checksums, rather than overwriting revised data.
5. Independent verification of any third-party archive before treating it as a complete replacement.

The most useful follow-up questions for ACF are the transmission dates of FY2023–FY2025 congressional reports, current full-time and part-time staffing, warehouse contract continuity, and the schedule for finalizing preliminary data.
